subject: Reserved capacity sizing — NeoForm memory/KV cache and quantization tradeoffs
messages:
From: Amit Shah <amit@neoform.ai>

Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>

Subject: Sizing ask — reserved pool for Llama-3-70B variant (64k) + KV cache

Hi team,

Thanks for the intro call yesterday. We want to move toward a reserved (dedicated) pool with Redwood for production inference. A couple of hard constraints from our side:
- Model: Llama-3-70B family (we'll run a main 70B dense variant and fall back to a quantized 70B-4bit for batch/rate events).
- Typical request profile (initial): 12 QPS sustained, 45 concurrent sessions at peak, average prompt+response = 800 tokens (prompt ~200 / response ~600).
- Context: up to 64k tokens (we rely on long-context summarization workflows); we expect many requests to reuse prefixes (long KV cache hits).
- SLO: median latency target 200–300ms for first token on the dense path; tail latency requirement is softer but we'd prefer <1s for 95th.
- Compliance: ability to run in dedicated VPC (not air-gapped yet).

Can you provide a sizing estimate: GPU types, memory per GPU needed for model + KV cache headroom, recommended pool size, and the impact of using int8 vs int4 quantized variants on both memory and expected throughput? Also call out any operational recommendations (KV offload, batching windows) that materially change capacity needs.

Attaching NeoForm_SLA_Reqs.pdf that lists our targets and initial traffic forecast.

Thanks,
Amit Shah
Head of ML Ops, NeoForm

Subject: Re: Sizing ask — reserved pool for Llama-3-70B variant (64k) + KV cache

Amit — thanks for the clear spec and the SLA doc. Looping in Marcus (serving/runtime) and Karthik (capacity planning) to get a consolidated estimate.

High level findings (summary) — see attached spreadsheet for line-by-line math: 20260120-neoform-sizing-estimate.xlsx
- Baseline memory footprint (70B dense) at 32-bit activation+weights mapping for our optimized runtime: ~55–60GB model+exec memory on GPU.
- With standard int8 weight + mixed-precision activations: model residency reduces to ~38–42GB. Int4 variants (weight-only quantization with activation FP16) push model residency down to ~28–32GB but increase CPU/GPU kernel variance and may reduce single-stream tail latency in some cases.
- KV cache for 64k context: approximate per-session KV cache (key+value) = 64k tokens * 2 vectors/token * 16 bytes/vector (FP16) ≈ 2.0GB per full context. With compression and our prefix sharing heuristics, effective per-session average is closer to 0.6–0.9GB (because many requests reuse prefixes).
- For 45 concurrent long-context sessions worst-case (no KV sharing): KV = 45 * 2.0GB ≈ 90GB; realistic working set assuming 60% reuse ≈ 36GB.

Sizing recommendation (initial reserved pool):
- Option A (low-risk, performance-first): 6x A100 80GB-class GPUs (or equivalent Ampere/next-gen with >=80GB HBM) configured as a single pooled cluster. Each GPU can host one dense 70B instance (int8) plus ~10–12GB of KV cache for active shards before offloading. Account for model + runtime ~40GB + per-GPU KV headroom. This yields steady 12 QPS and handles 45 conc sessions with shared KV.
- Option B (cost-lean, hybrid): 6x 48GB GPUs + an additional NVMe-backed KV offload layer (fast NVMe SSDs on each node). Use int4 quantized model for lower residency (28–32GB) so model+runtime fits 48GB with limited KV-local headroom. This increases latency variance but reduces peak GPU count/cost.
- Option C (burst + fallback): 4x 80GB dedicated GPUs for dense, plus 4x 48GB quantized pool for overflow. Requests are routed by policy: latency-sensitive requests -> dense pool; batch/throughput requests -> quant pool. This reduces committed spend while preserving tail behavior.

Operational tips that materially change capacity:
- Prefix/KV sharing: encouraging client-side prefix canonicalization (or using our shared prefix cache) can drop KV working set by >50% for summary workflows.
- Aggressive batching for quantized pool: int4 backends can throughput-batch much better; expect 2–3x effective QPS per GPU relative to single-stream.
- KV offload: adding NVMe offload reduces required HBM headroom per GPU (moves cold context to SSD) but increases first-access latency by ~30–120ms depending on SSD tier.

Next steps: Marcus to validate microbenchmarks on our lab with your exact model artifacts; Karthik to convert these options into monthly reserved capacity costs and commit sizing. If you can confirm: (a) expected % of requests that are long-context non-shared, (b) willingness to accept small tail latency delta for int4, we can finalize a recommended reserved-pool SKU and provide contract options.

I attached an XLSX with the calculation and a short decision tree. Happy to run a quick workshop with your infra team.

—Irene
Irene Choi
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks Irene — this is very helpful. A few clarifications:
1) Long-context non-shared requests: we estimate ~30% of traffic will be unique long-context (i.e., not reusing cached prefixes). That was conservative planning.
2) We are okay with a 10–20% tail latency increase for int4 on the non-latency-critical paths (as long as median stays sub-400ms).
3) We prefer Option C (hybrid) if it comes with clear routing rules and automated fallback. Could you call out how warm-up / cold-to-hot migration of KV would behave in that split architecture?

Also procurement asked for an approximate monthly committed cost and a note of whether reserved capacity can be scaled at 30-day windows.

If you can send a short doc that calls out: recommended minimum committed pool, fallback routing policy, expected median/tail numbers for each pool, and a 30/60/90 day ramp plan, we can move this to our legal/procurement team.

Regards,
Amit

Amit — appreciate the quick follow. Short answers and next actions below.

Routing / KV warm-up behavior (high level):
- Routing: Redwood routing engine supports per-route policies. For your plan we suggest:
  1) route.latency_sensitive -> dense_pool (4x 80GB GPU nodes)
  2) route.throughput_pref -> quant_pool (4x 48GB GPU nodes, int4)
  3) fallback: if dense_pool at 90% util -> spill to quant_pool with a per-request downgrade header so app can decide to retry later.
- KV warm-up / migration: when a request first touches a previously cold segment, the serving runtime will load the relevant KV shard from NVMe offload into GPU HBM; subsequent hits are kept in LRU HBM until eviction. We provide metrics to track miss/hit rates. For hybrid pools, we keep a lightweight shared prefix index so identical prefixes requested in quant_pool can be promoted to dense_pool HBM when needed (background prefetch based on access frequency). Expect a cold-to-hot promotion penalty of ~80–150ms for the first access.

Committed sizing + ramp (proposal):
- Minimum committed: 4x 80GB dense + 4x 48GB quant (Option C) with an initial 60% headroom allowance. This supports the target 12 QPS sustained and 45 concurrency with your 30% unique long-context assumption.
- 30/60/90 day ramp: month 1 = 60% of committed (warm-up + pilot), month 2 = 85% (observability-driven scale), month 3 = 100% reserved activation. We can offer a prorated scaling window at 30-day intervals.

Pricing note (ballpark): monthly reserved charge for the proposed committed pool + standard support and observability is attached in the spreadsheet (line items by GPU class). We'll have a formal pricing quote from finance once you confirm the target committed pool.

Next steps: Irene / Marcus can run two microbenchmarks with your model artifact (dense + int4 build) — Marcus, can you run a 1-hour stress test targeting our 12 QPS pattern with a synthetic mix (30% unique long-context) and share the results by EOD Friday?

Amit — if you sign off on the minimum committed and ramp, we'll generate a commercial SOW and a 30-day scaling clause for procurement.

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Head of Customer Success, Redwood Inference
